The graph of the function $y={f}^{′}(x)$, the derivative of $y=f(x)$, is shown above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y={f}^{″}(x)?$
question.worked_solution:
First, if we denote $g(x)={f}^{′}(x)$ then ${f}^{″}(x)={g}^{′}(x).$ So, we need to sketch the graph of $y={g}^{′}(x)$ given the graph of $y=g(x),$ as usual.

Notice the following:

- At the stationary points, where the tangent line to $y=g(x)$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, we have ${g}^{′}(x)=0.$

- When $g(x)$ is increasing, we have ${g}^{′}(x)>0.$

- When $g(x)$ is decreasing, we have ${g}^{′}(x)<0.$

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below. Note that the stationary points were identified (approximately) from the graph of $y={g}^{′}(x)$:

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,0)$ | $0$ | $(0,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,2)$ | $2$ | $(2,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $g$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |
| ${g}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |

Additionally, the function $y=g(x)$ has inflection points at $x≈0.5$ and $x≈1.5.$ At the inflection points, we have ${g}^{″}(x)=0,$ so the tangent to the graph of $y={g}^{′}(x)$ must be parallel to the $x$-axis at $x≈0$ and $x≈2.$ 

We don't know the exact values of ${g}^{′}(0.5)$ and ${g}^{′}(1.5)$, but from the graph of $y=g(x)$ we find that the slope of the tangents to ${g}^{′}(x)$ at $x≈0.5$ and $x≈1.5$ are  negative and positive, respectively.  

Therefore, the graph of $y={g}^{′}(x)={f}^{″}(x)$ may look as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14190876/assets/4289eb05ab23d48f2727848724d3cd2f130cdb5fe9d92d569f3abd05b534c0e2.png)
